{{short description|Geometric space with seven dimensions}}
{{No footnotes |date= August 2026}}
'''Seven-dimensional''' ('''7D''') '''space''' is a sequence of {{mvar|n}} [[real number]]s (when {{nowrap|1= {{mvar|n}} = 7}}) that can be understood as a [[point (geometry)|location]] in [[dimension|{{mvar|n}}-dimensional]] space. Often such a space is studied as a [[vector space]], without any notion of distance. Seven-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] is seven-dimensional space equipped with a [[Euclidean metric]], which is defined by the [[dot product]].{{disputed-inline|date=November 2014}}

More generally, the term may refer to a seven-dimensional vector space over any [[field (mathematics)|field]], such as a seven-dimensional [[complex number|complex]] vector space, which has 14 real dimensions. It may also refer to a seven-dimensional [[manifold]] such as a [[7-sphere]], or a variety of other geometric constructions.

Seven-dimensional spaces have a number of special properties, many of them related to the [[octonion]]s. An especially distinctive property is that a [[cross product]] can be defined only in three or seven dimensions. This is related to [[Hurwitz's theorem (composition algebras)|Hurwitz's theorem]], which prohibits the existence of algebraic structures like the [[quaternion]]s and octonions in dimensions other than 2, 4, and 8. The first [[exotic sphere]]s ever discovered were seven-dimensional.

==Geometry==

===7-polytope===
{{Main|Uniform 7-polytope}}

A [[polytope]] in seven dimensions is called a 7-polytope. The most studied are the [[regular polytope]]s, of which there are only [[List of regular polytopes#Convex 4|three in seven dimensions]]: the [[7-simplex]], [[7-cube]], and [[7-orthoplex]]. A wider family are the [[uniform 7-polytope]]s, constructed from fundamental symmetry domains of reflection, each domain defined by a [[Coxeter group]]. Each uniform polytope is defined by a ringed [[Coxeter-Dynkin diagram]]. The [[7-demicube]] is a unique polytope from the D<sub>7</sub> family, and [[3 21 polytope|3<sub>21</sub>]], [[2 31 polytope|2<sub>31</sub>]], and [[1 32 polytope|1<sub>32</sub>]] polytopes from the E<sub>7</sub> family.

===6-sphere===
The [[n-sphere|6-sphere]] or hypersphere in seven-dimensional Euclidean space is the six-dimensional surface equidistant from a point, e.g. the origin. It has symbol {{math|''S''{{sup|6}}}}, with formal definition for the 6-sphere with radius {{mvar|r}} of
<math display="block">S^6 = \left\{ x \in \mathbb{R}^7 : \|x\| = r\right\}.</math>

The volume of the space bounded by this 6-sphere is
<math display="block">V_7\,=\frac{16 \pi^3}{105}\,r^7</math>
which is {{math|4.72477 × ''r''<sup>7</sup>}}, or 0.0369 of the [[7-cube]] that contains the 6-sphere.

==Applications==

===Cross product===

{{main|Seven-dimensional cross product}}
A cross product, that is a vector-valued, [[bilinear map|bilinear]], [[anticommutativity|anticommutative]] and [[orthogonality|orthogonal]] product of two vectors, is defined in seven dimensions. Along with the more usual [[cross product]] in three dimensions it is the only such product, except for trivial products.

===Exotic spheres===

{{main|Exotic sphere}}
In 1956, [[John Milnor]] constructed an [[exotic sphere]] in 7 dimensions and showed that there are at least 7 differentiable structures on the 7-sphere. In 1963 he showed that the exact number of such structures is 28.
